strengths: The paper proposes a clean unifying lens: TPV = Tr(H_eff C) separates model geometry (H_eff) from perturbation covariance (C), and connects label noise, SGD noise, quantization, and pruning under one first-order framework.
The empirical observation that TPV_train ≈ TPV_test holds across a large synthetic sweep and CIFAR/ImageNet models—even at very narrow widths—is interesting and could motivate follow-up work.
The pruning application (JBR) is simple and label-free, and the experiments show it is competitive with several baselines on CIFAR and ImageNet, illustrating potential practical utility.
The authors provide a relatively honest limitations discussion in Appendix C.2, explicitly identifying regimes where TPV stability breaks and where TPV loses discriminative power.
weaknesses: The proof of the central Theorem 2.1 is flawed. It asserts that Assumption A.2 on NTK stability of G_X implies an operator-norm bound on H_eff differences because H_eff and G_X share nonzero spectrum. This is not valid: sharing nonzero eigenvalues does not control the operator norm of the difference H_eff(w*) - H_eff(w0). A separate bound on ||J* - J0|| or on the Jacobian second moments is required. This undermines the main theoretical claim.

The bound |TPV_train - TPV_test| ≤ (2ε_NTK + o(1)) Tr(C) depends on Tr(C), which can grow with model size (e.g., Tr(C) = p δ²/12 for quantization). For overparameterized networks, ε_NTK Tr(C) need not vanish; the theorem can be vacuous without an additional assumption that Tr(C) is bounded or a normalized/relative-error version. The paper does not address this.

The label-noise theorem (Thm 3.2) is derived for a very specific minimum-norm stationary point of the linearized problem. It does not cover general label-noise training dynamics, and the real-data experiments perturb logits rather than true labels. The connection to practical label noise is therefore limited.

The claimed correlation between TPV and clean test loss is demonstrated mostly by varying width, which simultaneously changes model bias and capacity. Since expected test error decomposes as TPV + bias² (Eq. 3), the paper does not disentangle TPV from bias, nor does it control for logit scale/calibration across architectures. The evidence for TPV as a generalization metric is correlational and potentially confounded.

The surprising width=1 stability result may be affected by selection bias: runs violating the first-order check and runs where noisy loss does not decrease are discarded, but the discard rate is not reported. Extremely narrow networks may underfit and be insensitive to perturbations, making TPV_train ≈ TPV_test trivial in some regimes.

The pruning criterion JBR is essentially a label-free variant of the Jacobian Criterion (JC); when labels are correct and predictions are accurate, the scores coincide. The reported gains over baselines are marginal, and the paper does not establish clear superiority over state-of-the-art pruning methods. Moreover, the TPV stability theorem is not shown to apply to the functional u used for pruning, as the authors acknowledge.

Presentation issues: notation is overloaded (H_eff is used for both the test-distribution expectation and empirical train/test estimates), several figures are too small to read, and the main text contains overclaims such as “first result” and “state-of-the-art” that are not fully supported by the evidence.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code or data release is mentioned, exact architectures and random seeds are not fully specified for all experiments, and the pruning implementation is an external codebase whose modifications are not provided.

strengths: The paper introduces a unified perspective on parameter perturbations via the trace form Tr(H_eff C), connecting several noise sources (label noise, SGD noise, quantization, pruning) under a single local sensitivity framework.

The empirical study is broad, spanning synthetic data, CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet, multiple architectures, widths, and sample sizes, with careful controls (eval mode, fixed mini-batch order, first-order checks).
The observation that TPV stability holds even for extremely narrow networks (width=1) is striking and may motivate future theoretical work.
The paper provides detailed experimental protocols in the appendix, including hyperparameters and procedures, which aids reproducibility to some extent.
The label-noise TPV derivation (Theorem 3.2) gives a spectral expression that clarifies the role of Jacobian conditioning and test-distribution alignment.
The pruning criterion JBR is simple and label-free, and the empirical results suggest it is competitive with several baselines.
weaknesses: The main theoretical result (Theorem 2.1 / A.4) is essentially a straightforward consequence of the law of large numbers and assumed NTK stability. It bounds the difference between train and test TPV by Tr(C) times an operator-norm difference that vanishes only in the infinite-width, infinite-sample limit. This is a weak upper bound that does not explain the empirical stability observed at finite width and sample size, and does not provide a convergence rate or tightness.

The theorem is about the trace form Tr(H_eff C), but the experiments measure the original prediction variance Eq. 2 by retraining. The paper does not establish that the trace approximation is accurate in the regimes where stability is claimed, especially at width=1 or for large perturbations. The theory therefore does not directly support the empirical claims.

The claimed 'first result' is overstated: any i.i.d. train/test average of a fixed function (here H_eff at w0) converges to the same population quantity by LLN; the NTK stability assumption reduces the trained case to the initialization case. The novelty is limited.

The empirical TPV stability at width=1 contradicts the theorem's requirement of infinite width, and the authors acknowledge this but offer no theoretical explanation. This undermines the central claim that TPV stability is a consequence of overparameterization.

The label-noise TPV (Theorem 3.2) is not computable for modern deep networks due to extreme ill-conditioning of the Jacobian, as the authors admit (Appendix C.3.3). This severely limits the practical utility of the theoretical object and its role as a 'practical' framework.

The pruning method JBR is nearly identical to the existing Jacobian Criterion (JC); the authors admit they coincide when labels are correct and predictions are accurate. The 'label-free' advantage is marginal because labels are available during pruning. The empirical gains are not clearly significant (only figures, no tables, no statistical tests), and comparisons omit recent state-of-the-art pruning methods.

The correlation between TPV and test loss is shown only qualitatively; no correlation coefficients, confidence intervals, or controls for confounding factors (e.g., width, capacity) are provided. It is unclear whether TPV provides information beyond simpler measures such as weight norm or Hessian trace.

Presentation is poor: numerous typos, inconsistent citations (e.g., 'Keskar & et al., 2017', 'Arora et al., 2024' for a 2019 paper, reference list mismatches), confusing notation (e.g., δ_u^T δ_u in Eq. 16), and missing details in main text. This makes the paper hard to follow and verify.

The experimental protocol discards runs that violate a first-order check, which may bias the results toward stability. The number of discarded runs and the robustness of the conclusions to this filtering are not reported.

Reproducibility is limited: no code or model checkpoints are provided, and some procedures (e.g., turning off mini-batch shuffling, eval mode) are non-standard and may be difficult to replicate exactly.

The paper overclaims significance: it frames TPV as a 'unifying lens' and a 'foundation' for future work, but the actual contributions are incremental, and the limitations (e.g., non-applicability to finite-width, computational intractability) are not adequately addressed.

strengths: Introduces a coherent local sensitivity framework, TPV = Tr(H_eff C), that cleanly separates model geometry from perturbation covariance and unifies label noise, SGD noise, quantization noise, and pruning as parameter-perturbation mechanisms.

Provides a theoretical trace-stability result with a proof in the appendix, plus extensive synthetic and CIFAR-10/100/ImageNet experiments showing train/test TPV agreement and correlation with clean test loss across widths and architectures.

The paper is generally well-organized and gives substantial experimental details in the appendix, including hyperparameters, perturbation protocols, and first-order validity checks for synthetic experiments.

The pruning application, JBR, is simple, label-free with respect to ground-truth labels, and reported to match or exceed several structured-pruning baselines on CIFAR and ImageNet, suggesting practical utility.

Limitations and pathological regimes are discussed honestly, including cases where TPV stability breaks and where the trace-stability theorem does not directly apply (e.g., the probability functional used for pruning).
The TPV lens is potentially useful for fine-grained robustness analysis of a fixed trained model under specific post-training or near-convergence perturbations.
weaknesses: The central TPV trace-stability theorem is relatively weak and unsurprising: it follows from NTK stability plus a law of large numbers at initialization, and the bound scales with Tr(C), so it can become vacuous for large perturbations. The paper itself shows stability breaks for large noise and low n, and the theorem does not explain the striking empirical stability at width 1.

The novelty of the core object is limited: first-order prediction variance and trace forms like Tr(H_eff C) already appear in prior work on SGD noise, Fisher/Hessian approximations, and flat-minima analyses. The main contribution is the framing/unification rather than a fundamentally new quantity or a deep new theorem.

Theorem 3.2 for label noise assumes a minimum-norm stationary point of a linearized model, but there is little evidence that SGD reaches such a solution in practice. For real data, exact linearized TPV is numerically intractable, so empirical validation uses MSE fine-tuning on noisy logits with proximity regularization, which is not the same as label noise or min-norm interpolation.

The SGD-noise and quantization results are essentially re-derivations or approximations of known curvature-noise relationships, with several simplifying assumptions (dropping 1/n^2 terms, i.i.d. residuals, H_eff ≈ Hessian, small learning rate). No dedicated experiments are provided for these perturbation sources.

The claim that TPV provides a new way to gauge generalization is supported mainly by correlational evidence. There is no comparison to alternative complexity measures such as Hessian trace, sharpness, Jacobian norm, or Fisher trace, so it is unclear whether TPV adds predictive value beyond width or capacity.

JBR is a small variant of the Jacobian Criterion: it replaces ground-truth labels with the model's predicted class for confident samples. The pruning results are shown only in plots without numerical tables, error bars, or significance tests, making the size and robustness of improvements difficult to assess.

The paper states that TPV is a 'fully label-free object', but this is not accurate for all perturbation mechanisms: SGD noise covariance depends on residual variance and hence labels, and label-noise covariance may require knowing the noise variance. Label-free claims are strongest only for H_eff and the JBR criterion.

Presentation and reproducibility have issues: several citation year mismatches (e.g., Chen et al., 2025 vs. 2023; Bar et al., 2024 vs. 2020; Arora et al., 2024 vs. 2019), some notation/typo problems, low-resolution figures, and no code or reproducibility statement despite extensive hyperparameter descriptions.

strengths: The paper introduces an interesting unifying perspective: Test Prediction Variance (TPV) as a local prediction-variance functional with a trace form Tr(H_eff C), which conceptually places SGD noise, label noise, quantization, and pruning under one framework.

The empirical TPV stability results are striking and extensive: across synthetic data, CIFAR-10/100, and various widths, training-set TPV tracks test-set TPV closely, even at width=1, and is decoupled from the generalization gap.

The derivation of label-noise TPV in the nonlinear case (Theorem 4.2) provides a spectral characterization connecting label-noise sensitivity to the Jacobian singular values and the test-distribution Jacobian alignment, recovering benign overfitting as a special case.
The proposed JBR pruning criterion is practical and matches or exceeds seven baselines on CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet without fine-tuning.

The paper explores several practical applications of training-set TPV for model selection, including in-distribution recipe selection, cross-architecture selection, transfer learning with label noise, and robustness-aware recipe selection.
The limitations and pathological regimes are discussed, and the authors are transparent about the heuristic nature of the label-noise TPV estimation algorithm.
weaknesses: The central theoretical result (Theorem 3.1 / A.5) is not soundly established. The derived upper bound is |TPV_train - TPV_test| ≤ Tr(C) * ((n_tr+n_te)/p * ε_NTK + o_{n_tr,n_te}(1)). For isotropic C = σ² I_p, this becomes σ² (n_tr+n_te) ε_NTK + σ² p * o(1). In the overparameterized regime p → ∞ while n is typically fixed, the term σ² p * o(1) does not vanish, making the bound vacuous. The theorem therefore does not prove the claimed convergence of training-set TPV to test-set TPV in the overparameterized limit.

The proof uses a very loose trace inequality |Tr(B)| ≤ p ||B||_op, whereas the trace difference between two sample averages of rank-one Jacobian outer products could be bounded directly via a scalar law of large numbers (as O(1/√n)). This loose bound is the source of the non-vanishing term and obscures the actual behavior. As written, the theorem does not support the strong claim of 'first theoretical result' that training-set TPV is a reliable test-time estimator irrespective of generalization.

The theorem assumes an isotropic perturbation covariance C = σ² I_p. However, the most interesting perturbations—label noise and SGD noise—induce anisotropic C. The theory therefore does not directly justify the applications that rely on label-noise or SGD-noise TPV.

The empirical stability holds even at width=1, far outside the overparameterized regime assumed by the theorem. This suggests that the theorem is not the correct explanation for the observed stability and that the theoretical contribution is disconnected from the empirical phenomenon it aims to explain.

The label-noise TPV estimation algorithm used in experiments does not directly estimate the theoretical object from Theorem 4.2. It perturbs logits with Gaussian noise and fine-tunes on MSE, which is a heuristic proxy for label noise. The paper acknowledges that direct computation of the linearized TPV is intractable for deep networks, but the surrogate's fidelity to the theoretical quantity is not rigorously validated.

The JBR pruning criterion is essentially a label-free variant of the existing Jacobian Criterion (JC). The paper itself notes that under correct predictions JBR and JC coincide. The theoretical justification for JBR within the TPV framework is also incomplete: the paper admits that the TPV Trace Stability theorem only applies to logits, not to the functional u = -log p_{c(x)} used in JBR.

The model-selection applications are limited to the low-training-loss regime and are much less reliable across architectures. The paper acknowledges that cross-architecture ordering is weaker, which restricts the practical impact of the proposed training-set-only model selection.

The paper contains several presentation issues and typos: e.g., Theorem 3.1 defines c1 with n_te twice instead of n_tr+n_te; Figure 2's caption describes Figure 1 incorrectly; some claims are overstated relative to the evidence. These issues reduce clarity and make it harder to assess the theoretical contributions.

strengths: The paper offers a coherent organizing lens: framing post-training robustness via the first-order trace form Tr(H_eff C) is a clean way to separate model geometry (H_eff) from the noise mechanism (C), and it usefully places SGD noise, label noise, quantization, and pruning under one template.

The empirical study of TPV stability is substantial and well-scoped: 324 synthetic configurations plus CIFAR-10/100 sweeps, spanning five orders of magnitude in TPV, with an explicit first-order Taylor validity check and a clear demonstration that stability breaks only at very small n_train.

The empirical two-phase (U-shaped) TPV-vs-test-loss relationship, and the argmax-TPV landmark along a single ResNet-18/BERT training trajectory (Figs. 7-8, 17-20), are genuinely interesting observations and are supported by within-architecture evidence.

The manuscript is unusually candid about its own failure modes (Appendix D.2 on interpolation/pathological regimes, the n_train=10 and large-sigma breakdowns, the weak cross-architecture selection). The limitations and impact statement are handled responsibly, and there are no apparent ethical concerns.
weaknesses: Limited originality relative to the stated contribution. The authors themselves note that variants of Tr(H_eff C) appear in Zhu et al. (2018), Thomas et al. (2020), and Bar et al. (2024), and that the SGD-noise-to-Hessian proportionality (Thm 4.3) and quantization result (Rem 4.4) are known (Wu et al. 2022; Mori 2022; Mandt et al. 2016). The novelty is largely a re-interpretation of a known first-order object rather than a new method or new understanding.

The central stability theorem (3.1) is weak and its assumptions do not match the empirical phenomenon it is meant to explain. In the NTK regime the trained network is effectively linear in w, so H_eff(w*;X) = (1/|X|) sum_x phi(x)phi(x)^T is just a sample estimate of the same population second moment for both train and test; train/test 'stability' then reduces to a law of large numbers and is essentially independent of width. This is consistent with the authors' own surprising finding that stability holds at width = 1, which the overparameterization/NTK framing cannot explain. The paper admits the gap ('stability holds far more broadly than the theorem requires') but never reconciles it, which undermines the theoretical claim that overparameterization is the operative mechanism.

The theory-empirics connection for the headline label-noise result is broken. By the authors' own admission (Appendix D.3.3), the exact linearized label-noise TPV (the object of Theorem 4.2) is numerically intractable—CG fails to converge, condition numbers reach 10^6-10^8. All empirical 'label-noise TPV' numbers therefore come from a heuristic perturb-and-retrain procedure (D.3.4) that is never validated against the theoretical quantity it purports to measure. The practical claims rest on an estimator whose correspondence to the theorem is unverified.

The pruning application (JBR) is marginal. The authors state JBR is 'very similar' to the Jacobian Criterion of Chen et al. (2025) and is in fact identical in the clean/correct-prediction case; the only difference is substituting predicted-class labels for ground-truth labels. Since JC is itself one of the baselines, the reported 'matches or exceeds all baselines' is a weak claim, and the actual pruning results are relegated to appendix figures (21-24) with no numerical tables.

Practical model-selection claims are heavily qualified and depend on a regime the user cannot verify. The TPV-test-loss correlation is only positive in the 'low training loss regime' and inverts under underfitting; the cross-architecture ImageNet ordering is admitted to be unreliable (Appendix I.3: 'cross-architecture model selection reliability using TPV... we leave this for future work'). This substantially narrows the claimed deployment value.

Presentation and correctness issues reduce confidence: the typo 'n_te + n_te' in the Theorem 3.1 coefficient (should be n_tr + n_te); a dangling reference to 'Theorem 2.1' in the Appendix D.2 summary where 3.1 is meant; inconsistent citation formatting ('Keskar & et al., 2017'); and a dense, hard-to-parse introduction whose five claimed contributions are only partly delivered.

strengths: Provides a genuinely useful unifying lens: the trace form Tr(H_eff C) cleanly separates label-free model geometry (H_eff) from the noise mechanism (C), and the paper shows how SGD noise, label noise, quantization, and pruning all flow through the same curvature–covariance interaction. As a conceptual framework this is coherent and reusable.

The empirical TPV-stability result is striking and well-demonstrated: across 324 synthetic configurations and CIFAR-10/100/ImageNet settings, spanning >5 orders of magnitude in TPV, training- and test-set TPV cluster tightly on the diagonal, hold even at width=1, and are decoupled from the generalization gap. Figures 1–3, 12–14 convincingly support this, and it is a non-obvious observation worth reporting.

The analytical derivations connect TPV to recognized phenomena: Remark 4.1 recovers benign overfitting in linear regression, Theorem 4.2 extends it to nonlinear networks via Jacobian spectral geometry (Σ B_ii/s_i²), and Theorems 4.3/4.4 recover the wide-minima hypothesis for SGD and quantization noise. The spectral emphasis (label-noise TPV dominated by small singular values vs. sharpness by large ones) is a clean, explanatory insight.

Practical demonstrations are provided and mostly convincing in-domain: JBR pruning matches/exceeds seven baselines on CIFAR/ImageNet, and the model-selection experiments (Figs. 9–11, 25) show that training-set label-noise TPV ranks recipes consistently with test performance within an architecture—including the nice contrast in Fig. 11 where sharpness fails to predict label-noise sensitivity.

The paper is unusually honest about limitations and failure modes: it explicitly documents the interpolation/large-noise regimes where stability breaks or TPV loses discriminative power (App. D.2), the cross-architecture weakness of model selection (App. I.3), and the theory-empirics gap. Reproducibility details (perturbation protocol, eval-mode, mini-batch shuffling, hyperparameters) are extensive and clear.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim does not underwrite the central empirical phenomenon. Theorem 3.1 requires an isotropic perturbation covariance and the overparameterized NTK limit, whereas the actual perturbations (label noise, SGD noise) are anisotropic and the stability empirically holds even at width=1. The authors themselves state the theory does not explain the broad empirical stability, so the 'first theoretical result' is largely orthogonal to the headline finding it is meant to justify.

Much of the observed 'stability' plausibly follows from i.i.d. sampling plus a shared perturbation δw rather than from overparameterization: since TPV is an expectation over the data distribution and train/test inputs are drawn from the same D, train and test estimates of the same quantity concentrate by a Law of Large Numbers regardless of width or generalization. The genuinely interesting geometric content—why the Jacobian second moment H_eff does not overfit—is neither isolated nor explained, which weakens the significance attributed to the theorem.

Limited novelty in the core object: Tr(H_eff C) is acknowledged to appear in prior work (Zhu et al. 2018; Thomas et al. 2020; Bar et al. 2024), and the 'unification' is largely a repackaging of known results (e.g., H_eff ≈ Hessian near minima underlies both Theorems 4.3 and 4.4). The contribution is therefore more conceptual framing than new machinery.

Applications are incremental. JBR is essentially a label-free variant of the Jacobian Criterion (Chen et al. 2025), differing only by using predicted rather than ground-truth labels (App. H.1), and it 'matches' rather than clearly outperforms baselines. Model selection works within architectures but is explicitly unreliable across architectures, limiting its practical reach.

Theorem 3.1 is stated as an upper bound of the form c_1 Tr(C) with c_1 = ((n_tr+n_te)/p) ε_NTK + o(1); with isotropic C this yields a term scaling as σ²p·o(1) that grows with the parameter count, so the bound is not obviously tight and does not establish a clean convergence rate. The main-text typo (n_te + n_te) and duplicated/mislabeled figures (Figs. 21–24 repeated; text references that do not match) further suggest presentation carelessness.
